content: The University of Toronto Joint Centre for Bioethics (JCB) is an academic research institution located on the downtown campus of the University of Toronto in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. It operates as a partnership between the university and 15 affiliated healthcare organizations within the Greater Toronto Area. The centre focuses on the study of ethical and health-related issues through research, education, and clinical activities, with the goal of improving healthcare standards both nationally and internationally. The JCB is composed of a network of over 180 multidisciplinary professionals, approximately 30 of whom work full-time in bioethics. This makes it the largest multidisciplinary group of in-hospital bioethicists in Canada. In 2002, the JCB was designated as the first World Health Organization (WHO) collaborating centre in bioethics in 15 years. The centre was originally founded in the 1980s as the Centre for Bioethics by Dr. Frederick Lowy, then Dean of the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Toronto, who also served as its first director. In 1995, the Joint Centre for Bioethics was formally established in partnership with four Toronto hospitals, under the leadership of Dr. Peter A. Singer, who served as director until 2006. The current director is Dr. Ross Upshur. Mission, Vision, Values, and Goals The mission of the JCB is to provide leadership in bioethics research, education, and clinical activities. Its vision is to serve as a model of interdisciplinary collaboration, fostering the creation of new knowledge and improving practices in bioethics. The centre values academic and clinical excellence, intellectual freedom, integrity, respect, inclusiveness, and justice. While the centre itself does not advocate for specific positions on ethical issues, its individual members may do so. The goals of the JCB include: Promoting interdisciplinary research and scholarship, linking education to research, and disseminating findings to improve policies and practices. Supporting undergraduate, graduate, and postgraduate educational programs in bioethics. Enhancing clinical ethics activities, including continuing education for healthcare providers, ethics committees, ethics consultations, and addressing specific issues within partner institutions. Encouraging collegial discussions on bioethics issues across its network and serving as a resource for media, policymakers, and community groups. Research The JCB emphasizes the application of theory into practice through interdisciplinary research. Its research projects aim to address ethical issues encountered in partner hospitals and disseminate findings to improve healthcare policies and practices. To date, JCB members have published over 500 articles and secured more than $20 million in research grants. Key Research Areas 1. Clinical Ethics: The JCB’s Clinical Ethics Group developed the PEACE (Project Examining Effectiveness in Clinical Ethics) initiative to identify good practices in clinical ethics. This study involved nine case studies across Toronto hospitals, examining perceptions of effectiveness and good practices from the perspectives of bioethicists, clinical staff, hospital management, and patients and families. 2. Consent, Trust, and Error: The JCB created the Aid for Capacity Evaluation tool to help healthcare workers assess a patient’s capacity to make treatment decisions. Other research explores ethical issues in surgical care, including trust in the surgeon-patient relationship, obligations of surgical teams, innovations in surgical care, and managing conflicts of interest in surgical research. The JCB also developed policies for error disclosure and reporting to improve patient safety. 3. Disability, Rehabilitation, and Continuing Care: Research in this area focuses on ethical issues in physical medicine, rehabilitation, and complex continuing care. Current projects include defining ethical issues in rehabilitation, the right to refuse life-sustaining treatment, capacity and consent in rehabilitation settings, relationships between patients and workers, social aspects of disabilities in parents and children, and exercise among individuals with HIV/AIDS. 4. End-of-Life Care: The JCB has contributed to end-of-life care research by developing patient-centered models of quality care, advance care planning models, and frameworks for addressing euthanasia and assisted suicide. The Ian Anderson Continuing Education Program in End-of-Life Care trains physicians in caring for terminally ill patients and aims to establish a national network of healthcare providers skilled in end-of-life care. 5. Ethics Education: Bioethics education is a required component for accreditation in Canada and is considered as important as clinical training. JCB research identifies strengths and challenges in bioethics education and assesses delivery methods to align the curriculum with the needs of medical residents, ensuring they acquire the skills to address ethical issues in practice. 6. Genomics and Global Health: The JCB addresses global health inequities, particularly the ethical challenges posed by the genomic divide between developed and developing countries. Projects include research on convergence genomics and the ethical, environmental, legal, and social implications of genomics and biotechnology across health, nutrition, agriculture, and environmental applications. 7. Organizational Ethics: The JCB explores ethical issues faced by healthcare organizations, strategies to address them, and the effectiveness of these strategies. Key issues include resource allocation, business development, charitable fundraising, treatment decision disagreements, access to care for the uninsured, risk disclosure, workplace ethics, and conflicts of interest. Publications focus on the ethical obligations of healthcare managers and practical solutions. 8. Priority Setting: The JCB collaborates with the Canadian Priority Setting Research Network to improve healthcare priority-setting processes. Its research focuses on enhancing these processes, sharing real-world experiences, and adopting a bottom-up approach to improve resource allocation. 9. Public Health Ethics: Following the 2003 SARS outbreak, the JCB investigated the ethical implications of infectious disease management. Research topics include pandemic influenza planning, quarantine ethics, priority setting, and global governance. The centre also engages the public in debates about ethical pandemic planning. Education The University of Toronto, through the JCB, offers undergraduate, graduate, postgraduate, professional, and continuing education programs in bioethics. The centre coordinates all its educational programs, which cover a wide range of bioethics disciplines. Graduate-level degrees include a Master of Health Science (MHSc) in Bioethics and a Collaborative Program in Bioethics (CPB) at the master’s and doctoral levels. Continuing Education Programs The Ian Anderson Continuing Education Program in End-of-Life Care, a joint initiative of the JCB and Mount Sinai Hospital, aims to train 10,000 physicians in end-of-life care. Seminars The JCB hosts weekly public seminars featuring local, national, and international bioethics experts who discuss a variety of bioethics topics. Governance The JCB is governed by an Advisory Council comprising representatives from the University of Toronto and its partner healthcare organizations. The council provides advice to the Executive Committee and the centre’s director. Membership is typically held by individuals affiliated with the university or partner organizations and is reviewed annually. Members are expected to contribute to the centre’s research, education, or clinical ethics activities and to acknowledge their affiliation in bioethics-related publications and presentations. Partnerships and Publications The JCB collaborates with various organizations and has produced numerous publications on topics such as pandemic preparedness, clinical ethics, and rehabilitation care. Many of its publications are available on PubMed.
